name: Regemmelech
interpretive_note: The Hebrew syntax of Zechariah 7:2 is debated: most translations (including NASB) read it as the town of Bethel sending Sharezer and Regem-melech with their men to Jerusalem to inquire of the priests and prophets, but some scholars instead read 'Bethel-sharezer' as a single compound name, which would make Regem-melech the primary envoy sent from Jerusalem rather than from Bethel. Scripture does not resolve which reading is correct.
source_summary: Along with Sharezer, sent (on the NASB's reading) by the people of Bethel to inquire of the priests and prophets in Jerusalem whether to continue the fasts of mourning kept since the temple's destruction, prompting an extended prophetic response from Zechariah.
family_friendly_summary: Regem-melech was sent, along with a man named Sharezer, to ask the priests and prophets in Jerusalem an important question: should the Jewish people keep observing the sad fasts they had kept for many years, remembering when their temple was destroyed and they were taken into exile? Now that many exiles had returned home and were rebuilding, this question mattered -- should the mourning continue, or was it time for something different? Regem-melech's simple errand led to a much bigger answer. God gave the prophet Zechariah a message in response, teaching that true fasting means nothing without justice, kindness, and obedience, and promising that one day mourning would turn to joyful feasting instead.
adult_story: Regem-melech appears once in Scripture, alongside a man named Sharezer, sent -- on the most common reading of Zechariah 7:2 -- by the people of Bethel to Jerusalem, 'to seek the favor of the LORD, and to speak to the priests... and to the prophets, saying, Shall I weep in the fifth month and abstain, as I have done these many years?' (Zechariah 7:2-3). The question concerned whether the fasts of mourning kept since the temple's destruction decades earlier should continue, now that the exile was ending and the temple was being rebuilt under Darius. Regem-melech's inquiry, brief as his own role in it is, prompted an extended response from the LORD through Zechariah spanning two full chapters. Rather than answering the calendar question directly, God rebuked the nation for fasting and feasting for their own sake rather than His, recalling how their ancestors' failure to practice 'justice and kindness' toward the vulnerable, not mere ritual observance, had led to the exile in the first place (7:5-14). Zechariah closes with God's promise that the very fasts in question would one day be turned into 'joy, gladness, and cheerful feasts' for a restored Jerusalem (8:19). Regem-melech himself never speaks again in the text, but his delegation's question became the occasion for one of the clearest post-exilic statements that God desires genuine obedience over religious performance.
